title: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market

topics.title: Demand and the law of demand

learn.hook: When mangoes first arrive in May they are costly, and your family buys just a few. By June the price drops and suddenly there are mangoes in every bag. That is demand at work!
points: Demand is the quantity of a good that buyers are willing and able to buy at a given price during a period of time. Wanting something without the money to pay for it is not demand.

Law of demand: other things remaining the same, when the price of a good rises, its quantity demanded falls, and when the price falls, the quantity demanded rises. Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.
A demand schedule is a table of prices and quantities demanded. Drawn on a graph, it gives a demand curve that slopes downward from left to right.
Besides its own price, demand also depends on buyers' income, prices of related goods, tastes and season, and what buyers expect about future prices.
Related goods can be substitutes, used in place of each other (tea and coffee), or complements, used together (cricket bat and ball).

example.q: Think it through: In a Lucknow fruit market, buyers purchase 10 kg of mangoes a day at ₹100 per kg, 20 kg at ₹80, 35 kg at ₹60 and 50 kg at ₹40. What does this schedule show?
steps: As the price falls from ₹100 to ₹40 per kg, the quantity bought rises from 10 kg to 50 kg.
Price and quantity demanded are moving in opposite directions.
A lower price makes mangoes more affordable and makes them a better deal compared with other fruits, so people buy more.
This is exactly what the law of demand predicts.
example.answer: It shows the law of demand: as the price falls, the quantity demanded rises.

learn.reallife: Big festival sales, cheaper vegetables at the end of the day in a mandi, and people buying more train tickets when fares are cut all show the law of demand.

games.title: Substitutes or complements?
items: Tea and coffee
Sugar and jaggery
Bus ticket and train ticket on the same route
Rice and wheat
Car and petrol
Cricket bat and cricket ball
Fountain pen and ink
Mobile phone and SIM card

games.title: True or false?
items: Demand means wanting something, even if you cannot pay for it.
Demand needs both the desire and the ability to pay.
Other things being equal, a fall in price usually raises the quantity demanded.
This is the law of demand.
A demand curve normally slopes upward from left to right.
It slopes downward, because more is bought at lower prices.
If the price of tea rises, the demand for coffee tends to rise.
Tea and coffee are substitutes, so some people switch to coffee.
An increase in income can increase the demand for many goods.
With more money, buyers can afford to buy more.
The demand for umbrellas is the same in every season.
Demand for umbrellas rises in the monsoon.

quiz.q: What does the law of demand state?
options: Price and quantity demanded rise together
Other things being equal, quantity demanded falls when price rises
Quantity demanded does not depend on price
Sellers supply more when price rises
quiz.explain: Under the law of demand, price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, provided other factors stay the same.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the law of demand with the law of supply

quiz.q: Ritu really wants a laptop but has no money and no way to pay for one. In economics, is this demand?
options: Yes, if the shop has laptops in stock
No, because demand needs both the desire and the ability to pay
No, because laptops are free goods
quiz.explain: Demand means being willing and able to buy at a price. A wish without the ability to pay is only a desire.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a desire alone counts as demand

quiz.q: The price of tea rises sharply. What is likely to happen to the demand for coffee?
quiz.explain: Tea and coffee are substitutes. When tea becomes costly, some people switch to coffee, so demand for coffee rises.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a price change of one good cannot affect another good

quiz.q: Cars and petrol are complements. If petrol becomes much more expensive, what is likely to happen to the demand for petrol cars?
quiz.explain: Complements are used together. Costlier petrol makes running a petrol car more expensive, so fewer people want to buy one.
quiz.mistake: Treats complements as if they were substitutes

quiz.q: When the price of mangoes falls from ₹80 to ₹40 per kg, the quantity demanded rises from 20 kg to 50 kg a day. By how much does the quantity demanded rise?
quiz.explain: The rise is the new quantity minus the old one: 50 − 20 = 30 kg.
quiz.mistake: Gives the new quantity, or the change in price, instead of the change in quantity
steps: Old quantity = 20 kg, new quantity = 50 kg

quiz.q: The demand for umbrellas and raincoats goes up every July. Which factor explains this?
options: A rise in the price of umbrellas
quiz.explain: Demand depends on season and tastes, not just on price. In the monsoon more people need rain gear, even at the same price.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only price can change demand

quiz.q: How does a normal demand curve look on a graph?
options: It slopes downward from left to right
It slopes upward from left to right
It is a flat horizontal line
quiz.explain: Because more is bought at lower prices, the curve falls from left to right.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the shape of the demand curve with the supply curve

quiz.q: Why do economists say 'other things remaining the same' in the law of demand?
options: Because the government fixes all other factors
To study the effect of price alone while income, tastes and other factors are held constant
quiz.explain: Many things affect demand. Holding them constant lets us see clearly how price by itself affects the quantity demanded.
quiz.mistake: Takes the phrase literally, as if other factors could never change

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "The samosa wala raised his price from ₹15 to ₹25. Will people buy more samosas or fewer? Why?"
teach.praise: Chirp! When the price goes up, people buy fewer samosas. Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions: the law of demand!
teach.nudge: So what happens to the number of samosas people buy when the price rises? And what is this rule called?

topics.title: Supply and the law of supply

learn.hook: Just before Diwali, a potter in Kutch works late every night making diyas. Why does he make so many more now than in March?
points: Supply is the quantity of a good that sellers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price during a period of time.

Law of supply: other things remaining the same, when the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises, and when the price falls, the quantity supplied falls. Price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.
Sellers offer more at higher prices because they can earn more profit and can cover the extra cost of making more. So a supply curve slopes upward from left to right.
Supply also depends on the cost of inputs (seeds, fuel, wages), technology, weather for farm goods, the number of sellers, and taxes or subsidies.
Stock is the total quantity a seller has. Supply is only the part of that stock offered for sale at a particular price.

example.q: Think it through: A potter offers 100 diyas a day when the price is ₹5 each, 200 at ₹10, 250 at ₹15 and 300 at ₹20. What does this show?
steps: As the price rises from ₹5 to ₹20, the quantity offered rises from 100 to 300 diyas.
Price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.
A higher price means more earnings for each diya, so it is worth his extra time, clay and fuel.
This matches the law of supply.
example.answer: It shows the law of supply: as the price rises, the quantity supplied rises.

learn.reallife: When onion prices shoot up, farmers plan to grow more onions next season. When cold storage or better seeds become available, the supply of potatoes rises.

games.title: Will supply rise or fall?
items: Farmers start using better seeds
A new machine makes bricks faster and cheaper
More farmers start growing tomatoes
The government gives a subsidy on fertiliser
A drought hits the onion-growing areas
The price of diesel for fishing boats rises
A pest attack damages the cotton crop
A new tax is put on each unit produced

items.q: Price rises: quantity supplied rises or falls?
Supply curve slopes upward or downward?
Floods damage the wheat crop: supply rises or falls?
Better technology: supply rises or falls?
Price of cotton seeds rises: supply of cotton rises or falls?
Stock is 500 kg, 300 kg offered for sale. Supply in kg?
Price and quantity supplied move in the same or opposite direction?

quiz.q: What does the law of supply state?
options: Other things being equal, quantity supplied rises when price rises
Quantity supplied falls when price rises
Supply does not depend on price
Buyers buy more when price falls
quiz.explain: Under the law of supply, price and quantity supplied move in the same direction, as long as other factors stay the same.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the law of supply with the law of demand

quiz.q: Which way does a normal supply curve slope?
options: It goes down and then up
quiz.explain: Sellers offer more at higher prices, so the supply curve rises from left to right.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the supply curve with the downward-sloping demand curve

quiz.q: A severe drought hits the onion-growing regions of Maharashtra. What happens to the supply of onions?
quiz.explain: Farm output depends on weather. A drought means a smaller harvest, so fewer onions are available for sale.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that weather affects the supply of farm goods

quiz.q: A new machine lets a brick kiln make bricks faster at a lower cost. What is likely to happen to the supply of bricks?
quiz.explain: Better technology lowers the cost of production, so producers can offer more bricks at each price.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that better technology lowers costs and raises supply

quiz.q: A rice trader has 500 kg of rice in his godown. At today's price he offers 300 kg for sale. What is his supply of rice at this price?
quiz.explain: Supply is only the quantity actually offered for sale at a given price, which is 300 kg. The 500 kg is his stock.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the stock a seller holds with the supply offered for sale

quiz.q: When the price of a diya rises from ₹10 to ₹20, a potter increases his supply from 200 to 300 diyas a day. By how many diyas does supply rise?
quiz.explain: The rise in quantity supplied is 300 − 200 = 100 diyas a day.
quiz.mistake: Gives the new quantity or the change in price instead of the change in quantity

quiz.q: Why do sellers usually offer more of a good when its price rises?
options: Because the good becomes a free good
Because a higher price means more profit and covers the cost of producing more
quiz.explain: A higher price makes producing and selling more worthwhile, so sellers expand their output.
quiz.mistake: Does not link supply decisions to profit

quiz.q: The price of diesel for fishing boats in Kerala goes up a lot. What is likely to happen to the supply of fish?
quiz.explain: Diesel is an input. When input costs rise, fishing becomes costlier, so less fish is offered at each price.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the cost of inputs affects supply

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: "Why does the potter make so many more diyas when the price goes up before Diwali?"
teach.praise: Tweet! A higher price means more profit, so sellers offer more. Price and quantity supplied go up together: the law of supply!
teach.nudge: But what does the potter gain when the price is higher? Why would he want to make more?

topics.title: Market equilibrium: where demand meets supply

learn.hook: Nobody in the sabzi mandi announces the price of tomatoes on a loudspeaker, yet by mid-morning almost everyone is paying about the same price. Who decided it?
points: The market price is set by the meeting of demand (buyers) and supply (sellers).
Equilibrium price is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. At this price the market 'clears': there is no extra unsold stock and no buyer left unable to buy at that price.
If the price is above equilibrium, quantity supplied is more than quantity demanded. This surplus (excess supply) pushes sellers to cut the price.
If the price is below equilibrium, quantity demanded is more than quantity supplied. This shortage (excess demand) pushes the price up.
When demand rises (for example, sweets at Diwali) the equilibrium price rises. When supply rises (for example, a bumper harvest) the equilibrium price falls.

example.q: Think it through: Tomatoes in a mandi. At ₹20 per kg, buyers want 100 kg and sellers offer 40 kg. At ₹30: 80 kg and 60 kg. At ₹40: 60 kg and 60 kg. At ₹50: 40 kg and 80 kg. Find the equilibrium.
steps: Look for the price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
At ₹40 per kg, both are 60 kg.
At ₹20 or ₹30 there is a shortage, so the price would be pushed up.
At ₹50 there is a surplus of 80 − 40 = 40 kg, so sellers would cut the price.
example.answer: The equilibrium price is ₹40 per kg and the equilibrium quantity is 60 kg.

learn.reallife: Flower prices jump before festivals and weddings, while vegetable prices drop after a good harvest. In each case demand and supply move the price.

games.title: How a shortage disappears
games.prompt: Put the steps in order, starting with a price that is too low
items: The price is below the equilibrium price
Buyers want more than sellers offer, so there is a shortage
Buyers compete for the goods and the price rises
Quantity demanded falls and quantity supplied rises
Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied at the equilibrium price

items.q: Demand 50 kg, supply 80 kg: surplus or shortage?
Demand 120 kg, supply 90 kg: surplus or shortage?
Demand 120 kg, supply 90 kg: shortage of how many kg?
Demand 40, supply 100: surplus of how many units?
Demand equals supply: what is this price called?
There is a surplus: will price rise or fall?
There is a shortage: will price rise or fall?

quiz.q: What is the equilibrium price?
options: The highest price a seller can charge
The price fixed by the shopkeeper alone
The lowest price in the market
The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
quiz.explain: Equilibrium means balance. At this price, the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer.
quiz.mistake: Thinks one side, the seller or the buyer, alone fixes the price

quiz.q: At ₹20 a dozen, buyers want 90 dozen bananas and sellers offer 30. At ₹30, buyers want 60 and sellers offer 60. At ₹40, buyers want 40 and sellers offer 80. What is the equilibrium price?
quiz.explain: At ₹30 a dozen, quantity demanded and quantity supplied are both 60 dozen.
quiz.mistake: Picks a price where demand and supply are not equal

quiz.q: If the price in a market is above the equilibrium price, what happens?
options: There is a surplus of goods
There is a shortage of goods
Buyers want more than sellers offer
quiz.explain: Above equilibrium, sellers offer more than buyers want, so unsold goods pile up. That is a surplus.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up surplus and shortage

quiz.q: At ₹50 per kg, buyers want 40 kg of tomatoes but sellers offer 80 kg. How large is the surplus?
quiz.explain: Surplus = quantity supplied − quantity demanded = 80 − 40 = 40 kg.
quiz.mistake: Adds the quantities or gives one of them instead of the difference
steps: Quantity supplied = 80 kg, quantity demanded = 40 kg

quiz.q: Before Diwali, many more families want to buy sweets, while supply does not change. What happens to the price of sweets?
quiz.explain: A rise in demand with the same supply creates a shortage at the old price, so the equilibrium price goes up.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that a rise in demand pushes the price up

quiz.q: A bumper onion harvest brings far more onions to the mandi while demand stays the same. What happens to the price of onions?
quiz.explain: A rise in supply with the same demand creates a surplus at the old price, so sellers lower the price.
quiz.mistake: Thinks more supply leads to higher prices

quiz.q: When there is a shortage (excess demand) in a market, what usually happens to the price?
quiz.explain: When buyers want more than is available, they compete for the goods and sellers can raise the price until the shortage disappears.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up what happens in a shortage and in a surplus

quiz.q: Every evening, a fruit seller is left with a big pile of unsold mangoes. What should he most likely do to sell them?
options: Keep the same price and wait
quiz.explain: Unsold stock shows a surplus: his price is above equilibrium. Cutting the price will make buyers purchase more.
quiz.mistake: Thinks raising the price will help sell a surplus

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: "Nobody announces the price of tomatoes in the mandi. So how does the market decide it?"
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! The price settles where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer. That is the equilibrium price!
teach.nudge: You told me about one side of the market. What about the other side, and where do the two meet?
